preamble: Voicing of the voiceless postalveolar affricate [tʃ] to [dʒ], typically in weak positions: between vowels, after an unstressed vowel, or (in Turkic) after an originally long vowel. Late Middle English voiced [tʃ] in unstressed final syllables (knowleche > knowledge, -wich place names), and the Oghuz Turkic languages voiced Proto-Turkic *č intervocalically and, in Azerbaijani and Ottoman, also word-finally.

examples.from: Middle English knoweleche, knowleche 'knowledge' (< late Old English cnāwelǣċ)
examples.note: [tʃ] voiced to [dʒ] in the unstressed final syllable.
The unstressed -wich [wiːtʃ] element shows the same voicing, also heard as a variant in Greenwich /ˈɡrɛnɪdʒ/.
Intervocalic *č after an originally long vowel became [dʒ] (Old Anatolian Turkish acu); Karluk and Kipchak keep [tʃ] (Uzbek achchiq, Tatar ачы).
Synchronic alternation: stem-final ç voices before a vowel-initial suffix. Ottoman Turkish had voiced ağac even in the nominative.
Word-final *č voiced in Azerbaijani, while Turkmen agaç, Uzbek yogʻoch and Kazakh ағаш keep a voiceless reflex.

sources: Göksel, A., & Kerslake, C. (2005). Turkish: A Comprehensive Grammar. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203340769
